findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Housing Strategy 2026-2031
findings.headline: Council forecasts 75 affordable homes in 2026/27 and 90 in 2027/28, against an assessed need of 468 a year
findings.detail: The paper states the forecasts would meet only around 16–19% of assessed annual need. It attributes the shortfall to the number and scale of eligible sites, viability pressures, build-out rates and market conditions.
findings.matters: A supply gap of this size shows how far affordable delivery depends on Section 106 and Registered Provider investment rather than council-funded building, which other councils will also be relying on.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Housing Strategy 2026-2031
findings.headline: Local Housing Allowance gap to two-bed market rent rose from £85 in 2021/22 to £314 in 2025/26
findings.detail: The paper says the widening gap has left benefit-dependent tenants unable to meet rent requirements, which limits the private rented sector as a homelessness exit route and pushes households towards social housing.
findings.matters: The gap determines whether the Council can discharge homelessness duties into the private rented sector at a cost below temporary accommodation, a point that is directly relevant to council spend.
findings.quote: the gap between market rent for a two bed property in 2021/22 was £85, by 2025/26 this had risen to £314

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Housing Strategy 2026-2031
findings.headline: Council is using part of its £0.5 million homelessness prevention budget pledge to recruit two Homelessness Prevention Officers
findings.detail: The officers are to focus on early intervention, mediation and targeted financial support, with the stated aim of moving from crisis response to planned support and preventing the need for temporary accommodation.
findings.matters: Ring-fencing a pledge to prevention, with the expected payback in avoided temporary accommodation cost, is a spend-to-save decision other finance officers may be evaluating.
findings.figures: £0.5 million budget pledge; two Homelessness Prevention Officers
findings.quote: Blaby District Council have recruited two Homelessness Prevention Officers

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Housing Strategy 2026-2031
findings.headline: Blaby District Council successfully prevented or relieved homelessness for 1,356 households between 2020/21 and 2025/26, peaking at 311 households in 2023/24
findings.detail: The paper credits tenancy sustainment, landlord negotiation, mediation, financial support and income maximisation. It also says prevention has reduced evictions from social housing through early intervention on rent arrears.
findings.matters: Prevention volumes are the activity measure against which temporary accommodation cost reductions would be judged, so councils comparing approaches will want the outcome numbers.
findings.figures: 1,356 households; averaging around 226 households each year; peak of 311 households in 2023/24
findings.quote: Blaby District Council successfully prevented or relieved homelessness for 1,356 households

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Housing Strategy 2026-2031
findings.headline: Average stay in temporary accommodation doubled from 11 weeks in 2020 to 22 weeks in 2024
findings.detail: The paper attributes the longer stays to households waiting longer for suitable permanent housing. Longer stays are said to increase the need for self-contained accommodation, which further raises costs.
findings.matters: Average length of stay drives the cost per household, so a doubling of stay length compounds any increase in placements, which is a useful benchmark for peers.
findings.figures: 11 weeks in 2020; 22 weeks in 2024
findings.quote: As households wait longer to access suitable permanent housing

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Housing Strategy 2026-2031

findings.detail: The paper links the rise in temporary accommodation spend to longer stays and states that the Council faces significant financial pressures as a result. It also says future proposals to raise temporary accommodation standards are likely to add further cost.
findings.matters: A tenfold-plus rise in a single demand-led cost line is the kind of trend a finance director needs to model, and other councils facing the same statutory duty will see the same exposure.
findings.figures: approximately £155,000 in 2020/21; more than £1,828,000 in 2025/26

findings.quote: Across the life of the 5 Year Capital Programme, it is forecast that just under £0.79m of capital expenditure can be met from the Council's own resources (e.g., capital receipts and reserves), and another £4.59m from capital grants and contributions. This leaves a projected borrowing requirement of £14.18m between 2026/27 and 2030/31.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) including Plan to Close Future financial Gaps
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review determined that Blaby has fared poorly, with impact masked by Business Rate income treatment in settlement
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review has not treated Blaby favorably. The negative impact of the review on Blaby's allocation has been partially obscured by the way business rate income has been handled within the three-year settlement. This masking effect creates risk that the true impact of the review will become apparent in future settlement periods.
findings.matters: A council that has 'fared poorly' in a major funding review faces structural disadvantage in future settlements; this may represent a permanent downward shift in available funding.
findings.figures: Blaby fared poorly from Fair Funding Review; impact partially masked by business rate treatment
findings.quote: Whilst Blaby hasn't faired well from the review the manner in which Business Rate Income has been treated within the Settlement has somewhat masked the detrimental impact.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) including Plan to Close Future financial Gaps
findings.headline: County Council funding cuts creating difficult-to-quantify increased demand for Blaby services
findings.detail: The document notes that Leicestershire County Council has publicly announced significant funding cuts over coming years. Whilst the district council can plan for obvious impacts, some effects are subtle and harder to quantify. The resulting increased demand for services is identified as a considerable risk to which 'financial values will be put as and when we are in a position to do so'—indicating current uncertainty about the scale of the impact.
findings.matters: County council retrenchment is already known to be happening; the council cannot yet quantify its financial impact, creating a hidden budget risk.
findings.figures: Funding cuts from county council; financial impact to be quantified
findings.quote: The County Council has openly illustrated the level of funding cuts that they will be required to make over the coming years. Whilst we can plan to mitigate any obvious impacts of this, some are more subtle and the increased demand that results from this is difficult to quantify financially.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) including Plan to Close Future financial Gaps
findings.headline: Food waste implementation required by April 2026 with modelled costs that may be exceeded once service goes live
findings.detail: The council is required to implement food waste collection by April 2026. Funding has been provided in the settlement but is not specifically identified. Officers have modelled costs for the service, but there is explicit risk that actual costs could exceed budgeted amounts once demand from residents is understood.
findings.matters: A statutory service starting mid-year with uncertain demand creates cost risk; if budgets are exceeded, the council must fund the overspend immediately.
findings.figures: Service implementation April 2026; costs modelled but subject to demand uncertainty
findings.quote: Funding has been provided within the Settlement; however, it is not specifically identified. Officers have modelled the costs of providing this service, however until the service 'goes live' and demand levels from residents are understood, there is a risk costs could exceed those budgeted.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) including Plan to Close Future financial Gaps
findings.headline: Homelessness costs rising with only partial mitigation through property investment funded by external schemes
findings.detail: The council reports a considerable increase in homelessness costs and acknowledges potential for further increases. Whilst additional budget allocation has been made and the council is investing in temporary accommodation properties using Local Authority Housing Fund and council investment, the underlying demand trend is uncertain.
findings.matters: Rising homelessness demand is placing pressure on budgets; if the trend accelerates, it could create an unplanned overspend in a key statutory service.
findings.figures: Considerable increase in homelessness costs; additional expenditure budgeted
findings.quote: We have seen a considerable increase in homelessness costs and whilst allowance has been made in the budget for additional expenditure there is the potential for costs to continue to increase.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) including Plan to Close Future financial Gaps
findings.headline: £700k budgeted 2026/27 and £700k provisional from reserves 2027/28 for LGR transition, with risk of exceeding Blaby's share due to unresolved cost-sharing
findings.detail: £700k is budgeted in 2026/27 for LGR preparation with a further £700k to be released from reserves in 2027/28. However, there is no agreement between Leicestershire authorities on how transition costs will be shared, creating explicit risk that Blaby's final share will exceed these provisional sums.
findings.matters: LGR is a structural change with uncertain financial implications; unexpected cost overruns could force the council to draw down reserves more heavily than planned.
findings.figures: £700k budgeted 2026/27; £700k from reserves 2027/28 (provisional)
findings.quote: These are provisional sums and currently there is no agreement between authorities in Leicestershire as to how transition costs might be shared to form the new unitary authorities. As such, there is a risk that Blaby's share of transition costs is greater than the amounts allowed for.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) including Plan to Close Future financial Gaps
findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility funding of £1.6m forecast to decline by 20-30% over MTFS period
findings.detail: £1.6m of EPR funding from Defra based on recycling tonnages is included in 2026/27 but at risk of substantial reduction. The council has modelled 20% reduction from 2027/28 and 10% reduction in following years, and notes MHCLG has raised concerns about the longevity of this funding stream. Future reductions could come from consumer deposit schemes reducing collected tonnages.
findings.matters: This represents a material and declining income source with uncertain future levels; the council may be forced to downscale operations to match funding.
findings.figures: £1.6m EPR funding 2026/27; 20% reduction modelled from 2027/28; 10% reduction in following years
findings.quote: Funding of £1.6m has been included in 2026/27 budget figures from Defra relating to the Extended Producer Responsibility for Packaging (EPR)... The MTFS has modelled for a reduction of 20% in EPR from 2027/28 and a 10% reduction in the years following.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) including Plan to Close Future financial Gaps
findings.headline: Business Rates funding uncertain from 2029/30 onwards despite three-year settlement protection
findings.detail: The three-year settlement protects 95% of historical business rate income through 2028/29, but there is substantial uncertainty about whether this protection continues beyond 2029/30. Transitional funding rises to £3.03m by 2028/29, indicating significant damping protection is masking underlying funding reductions.
findings.matters: Business rates are a core revenue source; if protection is withdrawn as planned, the council faces an immediate cliff-edge funding reduction in 2029/30.
findings.figures: 95% protection through settlement; transitional funding rises to £3.03m in 2028/29
findings.quote: Whilst the 3-year Settlement has protected 95% of the income historically generated through growth and the Business Rate Pool, it is unknown as to what extent this will be retained from 2029/30 onwards.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) including Plan to Close Future financial Gaps
findings.headline: Budget gap forecast to reach £2.6m in 2028/29, potentially £6.7m by 2030/31
findings.detail: The MTFS projects widening budget gaps over the forecast period. The council identifies £2.6m gap in 2028/29, rising to potentially £6.7m in 2030/31 if all transitional funding is lost. This represents a substantial and growing funding shortfall with high uncertainty beyond 2029/30.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council has a credible plan to close growing budget gaps and whether transformation initiatives are likely to succeed.
findings.figures: £2.6m budget gap 2028/29; potential £6.7m gap 2030/31
findings.quote: The MTFS suggests that there will be a budget gap of £2.6m in 2028/29 which could rise to £6.7m in 2030/31 of all transitional funding is lost.

findings.paper_title: Recommendations of the Cabinet Executive: General Fund Budget Proposals 2026/27 - Report
findings.headline: S151 Officer formally questions whether reserves are adequate given LGR costs and homelessness demand
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer (Executive Director) explicitly states in her formal Section 25 opinion: 'there is a question as to whether the reserves are sufficient to underpin future financial pressures' caused by LGR uncertainty and ongoing demand-led spending (particularly homelessness).
findings.matters: The council's chief finance officer has flagged reserve adequacy concerns in her statutory opinion—the strongest governance warning available; this signals financial stress ahead
findings.figures: Not applicable; qualitative governance concern
findings.quote: Given the uncertainty as to how the costs of implementation of LGR are to be funded and the continuing costs of demand-led services, such as homeless, there is a question as to whether the reserves are sufficient to underpin future financial pressures.

findings.headline: MTFS forecasts funding deficits of £3.7m–£6.7m by 2030/31 depending on transitional grant continuation
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy models a significant structural deficit opening within four years. If transitional funding (currently £3.04m in 2028/29) ceases entirely, the 2030/31 gap reaches £6.7m.
findings.matters: Looming structural deficit will require major intervention: service cuts, major council tax rises, or merger into unitary authority cannot proceed without fiscal restructuring

findings.quote: The transitional funding in 2028/29 is £3.04m, should transitional funding continue to be included the financial gap in year 2030/31 increases to £3.7m, if transitional funding were to cease this gap would increase to £6.7m.

findings.paper_title: Recommendations of the Cabinet Executive: General Fund Budget Proposals 2026/27 - Report
findings.headline: Council drawing £1.06m from reserves in 2026/27 to balance current budget
findings.detail: The council proposes withdrawing £1.004m from earmarked reserves (including £505.7k from NNDR Income Reserve) and £54k from General Fund Balance to support the 2026/27 budget. This includes draws to fund leisure contract income shortfalls and homelessness services.
findings.matters: Reserve draw-down to fund recurring operations signals inability to fund services from current revenues; reduces financial flexibility for future shocks or LGR costs

findings.quote: In 2026/27 it is proposed that the Council makes a contribution of £1,004,643 from earmarked reserves to support the budget

findings.headline: Defra Extended Producer Responsibility funding of £1.6m flagged by MHCLG as having uncertain longevity
findings.detail: The council includes £1.6m in 2026/27 from Defra EPR funding (up from £1.5m in 2025/26). However, MHCLG has formally raised concerns about whether this funding will continue beyond the current arrangement.

findings.quote: Comments made by MHCLG have raised concerns as to the longevity of this funding stream.

findings.paper_title: Recommendations of the Cabinet Executive: General Fund Budget Proposals 2026/27 - Report
findings.headline: Business Rates baseline reset permanently reduces council's retained income by 37% from £5.6m to £3.5m
findings.detail: The government baseline reset redistributes retained rates income by relative need. Blaby's retained business rates income drops materially. The council will no longer benefit from business rates growth in its district due to the reset.
findings.matters: This is a permanent structural loss of revenue-raising capacity; the council must either cut services or raise council tax to replace it
findings.figures: £5.6m (2025/26) reducing to £3.5m (2026/27 before £505.7k reserve draw)

findings.paper_title: Recommendations of the Cabinet Executive: General Fund Budget Proposals 2026/27 - Report
findings.headline: Adjustment Support Grant of £1.382m has no commitment beyond 2026/27, creating a funding cliff
findings.detail: The council received a one-off adjustment support grant to compensate for changes in the business rates settlement. The grant is explicitly for 2026/27 only, with no guarantee of continuation. The S151 Officer notes this has increased MTFS gaps for years after 2026/27.
findings.matters: The council is balancing its 2026/27 budget with ~£1.4m of one-off funding; losing this in 2027/28 will require immediate service cuts or reserves draw
findings.figures: £1.382m in 2026/27; no commitment beyond this year
findings.quote: There is no commitment that this grant will continue beyond 2026/27 and the Final Settlement shows this grant being for one year only, as a result the gaps in the MTFS for years after 2026/27 have increased.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Fleet vehicle replacement programme of £7.7m locks in multi-year revenue costs via borrowing and MRP at critical time
findings.detail: Essential fleet replacement totals £7.7m over five years, predominantly in years 2–5. This creates fixed revenue commitments through loan interest and Minimum Revenue Provision that will burden a budget already projected to have a £6.7m deficit.
findings.matters: Large, inflexible capital commitments lock in future revenue costs precisely when the council's budget position is deteriorating
findings.figures: Fleet Vehicle Replacement Programme: £7,740,000 over five years; peak year spend: £2,955,000 in 2030/31

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Council will transition from internal borrowing to external PWLB debt when rates fall to 5%, creating refinancing risk
findings.detail: The council is currently using internal cash reserves to fund capital spending (cheaper than external borrowing). However, it states this 'cannot be sustained' and will shift to external PWLB borrowing once rates fall to approximately 5%. This creates timing uncertainty about when £14.2m of new external debt will be drawn, plus rate refinancing risk.
findings.matters: Lenders need visibility of when external debt will be drawn and at what rates, as this determines future debt serviceability against an already-deficit budget
findings.figures: £14.2m total borrowing planned over five years; external borrowing threshold: approximately 5% PWLB rates

findings.detail: Unallocated reserves fall from £478k to £196k over the planning period—a loss of £282k of financial buffer. This occurs simultaneously with planned borrowing of £14.2m. The council will have minimal reserves to manage emergencies or unexpected costs while carrying significantly increased debt.
findings.matters: Declining reserves combined with rising debt worsens the council's financial resilience and its ability to weather shocks or service disruptions
findings.figures: Unallocated reserves: £478k (31/03/26) falling to £196k (31/03/30); total unallocated resources: £1,138k falling to £683k

findings.headline: Projected budget deficit of £6.7m by 2030/31 signals structural financial unsustainability
findings.detail: The council's Medium-Term Financial Strategy projects a significant budget deficit by the end of the five-year planning period. This deficit indicates the council will be unable to balance its budget through normal service revenues and will face difficult choices about service reductions, tax increases, or further borrowing.
findings.matters: A council projecting a structural deficit presents elevated credit risk to lenders and indicates the finance director faces severe financial stress within the planning period
findings.figures: £6.7m budget deficit by 2030/31
findings.quote: The MTFS predicts a budget deficit of £6.7m by 2030/31.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Blaby District Council Audit Completion Report
findings.headline: IT control weaknesses identified: third-party risk assessment process not implemented and MFA deployment incomplete
findings.detail: Auditors identified that the council does not have a process to assess cyber risk in suppliers and third parties either at procurement or during contracts. Additionally, phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication has not been implemented across all systems. These issues were carried forward from prior observations.
findings.matters: Weak IT controls and incomplete security implementation increase risk of data breach or financial system compromise, which could affect financial data integrity.
findings.figures: No quantified impact; findings categorized as Amber (developing) priority
findings.quote: The Council does not proactively perform sufficient and appropriate risk assessment of third parties to identify cyber threats and vulnerabilities.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Blaby District Council Audit Completion Report
findings.headline: Audit working papers were of mixed quality and required multiple clarifications from management
findings.detail: The finance team submitted working papers that were often incomplete or poorly documented, requiring the audit team to repeatedly request clarifications and additional support. This delayed progress and is attributed to the council having had no full audit since 2019/20. Examples include receiving spreadsheets without proper supporting documentation and needing to speak to various staff members to piece together single areas.
findings.matters: Mixed-quality working papers indicate internal control weaknesses in financial record-keeping and documentation; suggests the council may not have adequate controls over its financial processes.
findings.figures: No full audit since 2019/20 (gap of 5+ years)
findings.quote: Working papers received were of mixed quality. We experienced some occasions of needing to go back to management to clarify what we needed and to ensure that the quality of the working papers was appropriate. Given the Council has not experienced a full audit since 2019/20, this was expected.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Blaby District Council Audit Completion Report
findings.headline: Pension liability of £7.3m has no audit assurance and cannot be verified
findings.detail: The council's defined benefit pension liability stands at £7.3m, but the auditors have no assurance over opening balances or year-on-year movements because prior years were disclaimed. They deferred audit work on this until 2025/26 when a new triennial valuation is due. Without prior assurance, they cannot conclude on the material accuracy of the 2024/25 valuation.
findings.matters: A large contingent liability with no audit verification creates undefined risk to the council's financial position and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £7,308,000 defined pension fund liability; £7,459,396 total other long-term liabilities
findings.quote: This means we have no assurance on the movements in year and cannot gain sufficient audit evidence on the material accuracy of the valuation of the pension fund liability as at 31 March 2025.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Blaby District Council Audit Completion Report
findings.headline: Auditors disclaim their opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements due to prior year assurance gaps
findings.detail: The auditors cannot form an unmodified opinion on the 2024/25 accounts. Despite completing most work, they lack sufficient assurance on opening balances and transactions from four prior years (2020/21 through 2023/24) that also had disclaimed opinions. The statutory backstop date of 27 February 2026 prevented completion of all planned procedures.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means no independent verification of the council's financial position; lenders have no third-party assurance of the accuracy of reported reserves, assets or liabilities.
findings.figures: Four consecutive years of disclaimed opinions: 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24, now including 2024/25
findings.quote: Due to the challenges of undertaking an audit where the previous four years have been disclaimed, it has not been possible for us to undertake sufficient work to regain full assurance and support an unmodified audit opinion ahead of the backstop date of 27 February 2026.

findings.paper_title: Auditor's Annual Report Appendix A
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will divert management capacity from delivering planned savings until council merges in April 2028.
findings.detail: Blaby is one of seven Leicestershire councils developing proposals to merge into three unitary authorities, with transition April 2028. This reorganisation requires significant management time and external skills. The auditor specifically identifies that this may divert attention from delivering planned savings, making achievement of previously planned savings less likely.
findings.matters: The council's ability to bridge its £12.692m funding gap depends on delivering transformational savings. If management is diverted to reorganisation for three years, these savings may not be realised, worsening the structural funding position at a critical time.
findings.figures: Reorganisation runs 2025-2028; council ceases to exist April 2028
findings.quote: Plans and arrangements for reorganisation will take up increasing capacity of senior officers and this may divert attention from the realisation of savings plans or make the achievement of previously planned savings less likely.

findings.paper_title: Auditor's Annual Report Appendix A
findings.headline: Council's financial plan depends on £3.3 million of unconfirmed government damping that may not materialise.
findings.detail: To bridge the funding gap from the Fair Funding Review, the MTFS assumes the government will introduce a damping mechanism to smooth funding reductions over three years, providing £3.3m from 2026/27. The auditor notes this is not a confirmed or guaranteed amount. If damping is lower or does not occur, residual funding gaps would increase substantially.
findings.matters: The council's financial recovery plan relies on £3.3m of hoped-for government funding that is explicitly unconfirmed. If this does not materialise, the structural funding gap widens, forcing more severe service reductions or faster reserve depletion.
findings.figures: £3.3m damping assumption in MTFS from 2026/27 onwards
findings.quote: This is not a confirmed or guaranteed amount and would be expected to be in the form of additional funding.

findings.paper_title: Auditor's Annual Report Appendix A
findings.headline: Funding gaps totalling £12.692 million over five years will deplete reserves below the council's own policy minimum.
findings.detail: Budget gaps range from £1.1m in 2026/27 to £4.9m in 2029/30. After planned transformational savings and efficiency initiatives, residual gaps remain: £534k (2026/27), £336k (2027/28), £2.165m (2028/29), £2.737m (2029/30). The council has sufficient reserves to cover these gaps but only by falling below its policy range of 10-45% of net budget requirement.
findings.matters: Reserves provide the buffer to absorb unexpected shocks. Once depleted below policy minimum, the council will have no resilience against further funding cuts, inflation, or demand pressures.
findings.figures: Total funding gaps £12.692m over five years; residual funding gaps 2026/27-2029/30 total £5.772m after identified savings
findings.quote: This would still leave the general fund in a positive position, albeit, the reserves balance would fall below the Council's minimum requirements during this period.

findings.paper_title: Auditor's Annual Report Appendix A
findings.headline: Business Rates Baseline Reset in 2026/27 will cut council income by £3.924 million in a single year.
findings.detail: The council has benefited from significant business rates growth since 2013. A reset of the baseline in 2026/27 will eliminate this benefit. The Medium Term Financial Strategy shows business rates income collapsing from £5.511m in 2025/26 to £1.587m in 2026/27. The council plans to draw £860k annually from its NNDR income reserve but this leaves approximately £3m of the income loss unmitigated.
findings.matters: This represents a permanent structural loss of income that cannot be recovered. The council will need to either reduce services or draw down reserves to cover this gap, reducing its financial resilience.
findings.figures: Business rates income drops from £5.511m to £1.587m (£3.924m reduction); council budgets to draw £860k annually from NNDR reserve 2026/27-2029/30
findings.quote: The MTFS currently includes income from Business Rates of £5.511m in 2025/26 to £1.587m in 2026/27, which is a significant reduction.

findings.paper_title: Auditor's Annual Report Appendix A
findings.headline: Fourth consecutive year of auditor opinion disclaimer means accounts cannot be verified.
findings.detail: Due to cumulative effect of four prior years of disclaimed opinions, the auditor has been unable to obtain full assurance on opening and closing balances in key areas by the statutory deadline of 27 February 2026. The auditor expects to disclaim the opinion for 2024/25 as well, meaning the financial position cannot be formally verified.
findings.matters: A lender cannot properly assess the council's actual financial position without audited accounts. Four years of unaudited statements represents a material governance failure and means the council's reported reserves and financial position cannot be relied upon.
findings.figures: Fourth consecutive year of auditor opinion disclaimer
findings.quote: We therefore expect to disclaim our audit opinion.

findings.detail: The council acknowledges that work remains to ensure lower-level risks receive appropriate attention and are properly recorded in the I-Plan system. This suggests the internal control environment does not yet fully cover all risks across the organisation.
findings.matters: Weak risk management can allow financial or operational problems to surface unexpectedly; a lender would want confidence that the council's control environment is robust.

findings.detail: The council has shortened partnership terms for the Lightbulb Service and Housing Enablement Team (HET) due to the potential impact of Local Government Reorganisation (LGR). This means the council is planning for major structural change and faces uncertainty about future service delivery and financial arrangements from April 2026.
findings.matters: LGR would fundamentally restructure the council and affect its financial stability, borrowing capacity, and service continuity; a lender needs to understand the scale of this uncertainty and whether the council has a funding plan for the transition.

news_drafts.headline: Blaby holds £25.9m for investment against £4m of external debt, funding capital from its own cash
news_drafts.lead:
Blaby District Council had £4m of external debt, the total of all loans it owes, at 30 June 2026, and £25.9m available to invest, according to the quarter one treasury management update (how a council borrows, invests spare cash and manages the risks of both) put to its Council meeting on 22 September 2026. The debt figure excludes finance leases.

The council has paid for its capital schemes, spending on things that last, from its own cash reserves rather than by taking out loans. The papers call this an "internally borrowed cash position", and say the council has been in it "for several years". Using its own money instead of a loan saves interest, but uses up the cushion that cash provides.

Officers plan to keep to this approach while the rate the council earns on investments stays lower than the rate it would pay on borrowing. The report says "balances will need to be replenished at some point in the future, subject to expenditure demands". Officers monitor reserves, balances and cashflows closely to support the position, the paper says.
